verdict_reasoning: No objection survived at levels 1a, 1b or 2. The patch extends the existing vacuum BufferAccessStrategy to the GIN pending-list reads, adds no user-visible surface, and leaves the insert path and gin_clean_pending_list() unchanged. Confidence is low because the thread is three messages long and shows no measurements.

brief.title: Pass vacuum's buffer access strategy to GIN pending-list cleanup
brief.problem: When VACUUM reaches ginInsertCleanup(), the function reads the metapage and every pending-list page with ReadBuffer() and ignores the vacuum's BufferAccessStrategy. shiftList() does the same when it re-reads processed pages. The author first saw this as an inconsistency, and suggests it also causes extra evictions from shared buffers for other processes.
brief.proposed_design: ginInsertCleanup() and shiftList() take a strategy argument and pass it down to ReadBufferExtended. The three vacuum-side callers pass the vacuum strategy. The post-insert cleanup path and gin_clean_pending_list() pass NULL, so their behaviour does not change.
user_visible_surface: C API: ginInsertCleanup() in gin_private.h gains a BufferAccessStrategy argument.
author_claims: A test script shows the strategy changes how GIN pending-list cleanup uses the buffer cache.
It may reduce evictions of other processes' pages from shared buffers.
Other call sites keep their current behaviour.
ReadStream, as in 6c228755add, does not fit, because each pending-list page must be read to find the next block.
It could be backpatched as far as 14, but the author proposes it for master only.
brief.thread_state: Xuneng Zhou agreed with the rationale and with the point that ReadStream does not fit, and the author rebased to v2. Nobody has discussed backpatching, and the entry is still in Needs review.
unclear: The material gives no test numbers, such as buffer hits, evictions or vacuum duration, with and without the strategy.
The proposal does not say if a small ring buffer slows cleanup of a long pending list that would otherwise stay cached.
The thread does not say if gin_clean_pending_list() should also use a strategy.
The proposal does not say if any extensions call ginInsertCleanup() and would break when its signature changes.

Does the vacuum ring buffer slow cleanup of a long pending list, given that shiftList() re-reads the processed pages before deleting them?
Should gin_clean_pending_list() keep passing NULL, and what is the reason for treating it differently from the vacuum callers?
Do any known extensions call ginInsertCleanup() and need a change when its signature changes?

committability.owner_note: Someone who knows GIN fast-update cleanup and the vacuum buffer access strategy code would have to own it. The one reviewer in the thread agreed with the rationale only.
committability.liability: The owner signs for the buffer-cache behaviour of GIN pending-list cleanup under VACUUM, including any slowdown on long pending lists. The change is small and easy to revert on master.
committability.author_follow_up: The author rebased to v2 five days after v1 and moved the entry to the next CommitFest, which suggests continued attention.

priority.reason: The patch is 6.4 KB across three GIN files and adds no user-visible surface, so review is cheap. It benefits installations with large GIN pending lists; numbers from the test script would help a committer decide quickly.

provisional_note: Without the code, it is not possible to check that every pending-list read in ginInsertCleanup() and shiftList() receives the strategy, or that the NULL callers behave as before. The effect of the ring buffer on a long pending list is unmeasured.

precedents_retrieved.title: Eagerly evict bulkwrite strategy ring
precedents_retrieved.summary: Make the BAS_BULKWRITE buffer access strategy flush several dirty buffers in its ring at once, skipping buffers whose flush would require a WAL flush. This was meant as a first step toward combining writes and issuing them asynchronously, and gave about 15-20% faster parallel COPY FROM.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author withdrew the entry after moving all of its patches into the patch set in the separate write combining thread, so the work continues there. No reviewer objected to the design; reviews found only code issues, which the author fixed. Earlier the author noted that the gain from this patch alone might not justify committing it.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: All of the patches that implement the bulkwrite eager flush functionality are included in the patch set being actively updated in this thread [1] on write combining.

precedents_retrieved.title: use AV work items infrastructure for GIN pending list's cleanup
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch moves GIN pending list cleanup to an autovacuum work item, requested when the list reaches gin_pending_list_limit. Inserts and updates would then no longer pay for the cleanup.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Masahiko Sawada pointed out that work items run only after an autovacuum run, so the pending list could grow far past gin_pending_list_limit while the same work item is registered again and again. He suggested a soft limit and a hard limit, removal of duplicate work items, and skipping the item if autovacuum already cleaned the index. The author had no time to finish a revised version, so he marked the entry "Returned with feedback" and planned to resubmit.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
So if many insertions happen before executing the autovacuum
work item, we will end up greatly exceeding the threshold
(gin_pending_list_limit) and registering the same work item again and
again.

precedents_retrieved.title: New strategies for freezing, advancing relfrozenxid early
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch series lets each VACUUM choose a skipping strategy and a freezing strategy at the start, using a snapshot of the visibility map, so that unfrozen all-visible pages do not pile up until an aggressive VACUUM. A new vacuum_freeze_strategy_threshold GUC and reloption, default 4GB, makes VACUUM freeze eagerly in tables above that size, and a further patch avoids allocating new MultiXactIds during freezing.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Andres Freund posted a short test with transient data, cited in message #98, in which autovacuum wrote about 1.5x to 7x as much WAL with eager freezing. He argued that table size cannot tell VACUUM whether eager freezing is a good idea, and said he saw no alternative to reverting the commit. Robert Haas agreed that the scenario is common and objected to large behavior changes based on limited evidence. Peter Geoghegan reverted the commit and withdrew the whole series.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: The actual scenario he came up with is three lines of SQL, and it's nothing remotely obscure. That kind of thing is going to happen *all the time*.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert the GinMaxItemSize calculation so that we fit 3 tuples per page.
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert the GinMaxItemSize calculation so that we fit 3 tuples per page.
Reverted commit(s): Compress GIN posting lists, for smaller index size.
precedents_retrieved.objection:
Commit 36a35c55 changed the divisor from 3 to 6, for no apparent reason.
Reducing GinMaxItemSize like that created a dump/reload hazard: loading a
9.3 database to 9.4 might fail with "index row size XXX exceeds maximum 1352
for index ..." error. Revert the change.

While we're at it, make the calculation slightly more accurate. It used to
divide the available space on page by three, then subtract
sizeof(ItemIdData), and finally round down. That's not totally accurate; the
item pointers for the three items are packed tight right after the page
header, but there is alignment padding after the item pointers. Change the
calculation to reflect that, like BTMaxItemSize does. I tested this with
different block sizes on systems with 4- and 8-byte alignment, and the value
after the final MAXALIGN_DOWN was the same with both methods on all
configurations. So this does not make any difference currently, but let's be
tidy.

Also add a comment explaining what the macro does.

This fixes bug #12292 reported by Robert Thaler. Backpatch to 9.4, where the
bug was introduced.

precedents_retrieved.title: Add index scan progress to pg_stat_progress_vacuum
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds index vacuum progress to pg_stat_progress_vacuum, with counts of indexes to process and indexes processed, including indexes handled by parallel vacuum workers. Later versions keep worker progress in a hash table in the main shared memory segment, so the progress views can read it after a worker exits.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Andres Freund and Robert Haas objected to the use of the main shared memory segment and to the locking it adds to progress reporting, which is meant to be low overhead. They asked that workers pass data to the leader through the parallel vacuum's dynamic shared memory, and that the leader report it with the existing progress fields; Masahiko Sawada agreed. Greg Stark returned the patch because of these design changes.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
That is, I am imagining that you would want to use DSM to propagate
data from workers back to the leader and then have the leader report
the data using the existing progress-reporting facilities.

precedents_retrieved.title: Fix buffer pinning logic/visibility bugs in [SP-]Gist Index-Only Scans
precedents_retrieved.authors: Peter Geoghegan (pgeoghegan), Michail Nikolaev (nkey), Matthias van de Meent (mmeent), Mihail Nikalayeu (mihailnikalayeu)
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch fixes a race in GiST and SP-GiST index-only scans, where concurrent VACUUM can remove a TID and set the visibility map bit before the scan checks it, so a dead tuple is returned. Later versions drop the idea of holding pins on index pages: they add a table AM API (table_index_vischeck_tuples) so the index AM checks the visibility map while it still holds the page pin, and they also change nbtree to use it.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages do not show why. The last visible message (v14, December 2025) only fixes a CFBot failure, and the entry was withdrawn about six months later with no visible objection or explanation. The author had moved a backpatchable version of the fix to a separate thread.

precedents_retrieved.title: Add last_vacuum_index_scans in pg_stat_all_tables
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds a last_vacuum_index_scans column to pg_stat_all_tables that shows how many index scans the last vacuum of each table needed. The author meant it as a signal for raising maintenance_work_mem or autovacuum_work_mem.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Alvaro Herrera objected that the column keeps only the last vacuum's value, unlike other stats counters, which are all additive; he and Peter Geoghegan said a history of vacuum runs would be more useful. Fujii Masao asked whether one global counter in a pg_stat_vacuum view would be enough, and Alvaro later doubted the tuning value because autovacuum memory is capped at 1 GB. The author did not resolve these points, and the visible thread ends with a request for a rebased patch that got no reply before the entry was withdrawn.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: No other stats counter works that way; they are all additive.

precedents_retrieved.objection:
The reverted changes were intended to force a choice of whether any
newly-added BufferGetPage() calls needed to be accompanied by a
test of the snapshot age, to support the "snapshot too old"
feature.  Such an accompanying test is needed in about 7% of the
cases, where the page is being used as part of a scan rather than
positioning for other purposes (such as DML or vacuuming).  The
additional effort required for back-patching, and the doubt whether
the intended benefit would really be there, have indicated it is
best just to rely on developers to do the right thing based on
comments and existing usage, as we do with many other conventions.

This change should have little or no effect on generated executable
code.

Motivated by the back-patching pain of Tom Lane and Robert Haas

roaster_notes.note: The precedent search returned no earlier proposal with the same or a similar idea. The thread does not point to any earlier discussion beyond commit 6c228755add, which message #1 and message #2 cite as related work, not as a rejected attempt. So no prior rejection reason applies here.

From the standards and compatibility angle there is nothing to object to. The patch adds no SQL syntax, GUC, catalog object or psql change. Nothing new needs to round-trip through pg_dump. Existing queries and scripts see no different results, and gin_clean_pending_list() keeps its current behaviour. The only signature change is ginInsertCleanup() in the private header gin_private.h, and the proposal targets master only, so back-branch ABI is not affected. Buffer-cache effects belong to other angles.

The patch only changes which buffer access strategy is used when reading GIN pages. It adds no on-disk format, WAL record, catalog, wire protocol or replication change. The ginInsertCleanup() signature change is in the private header gin_private.h and is proposed for master only, so ABI matters only if someone later asks for a backpatch.

The patch has no privilege or exposure aspect. It passes the existing vacuum BufferAccessStrategy into GIN pending-list cleanup, changes no user-callable interface or permission check, and leaves gin_clean_pending_list() and the insert path unchanged. A ring buffer limits shared-buffer use, so it adds no denial-of-service path for unprivileged users.

From the maintenance and fit angle there is no objection. The patch follows the existing practice of passing the vacuum strategy to index reads, adds no per-tuple or per-query cost for anyone outside VACUUM, and changes only a function declared in gin_private.h, on master only. The open points are measurement questions for the performance angle: no numbers are given, and the effect of a small ring on a long pending list is unknown.

No existing feature covers this. The pending-list reads ignore the vacuum strategy, so vacuum_buffer_usage_limit has no effect on them. The patch extends the existing BufferAccessStrategy mechanism and adds no second one, and an extension could not change how core GIN reads these pages.

The material shows no field reports or numbers. But this is a consistency fix that makes GIN pending-list cleanup follow the same vacuum BufferAccessStrategy other index vacuum code uses. It adds no user-visible surface, and its only cost is a C signature change, so a demand objection does not apply.
